content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
This paper proposes to learn attention among pairs of input units (they call these entities) as a matrix of attention values. These when aggregated along a row gives a summary of related entities for each input entity, and when aggregated overall gives the 'soft' entity-pairs in an input.  They apply it on four image-related tasks: object detection, categorization, relation , and scene detection and one document classification task.  Direct supervision for learning the entity-pair attention is only available from the relation proposal task.  They also induce indirect supervision from the object detection task using co-occurrence of objects in an image.  For text they hypothesize attention pair supervision based on POS tags.  Their experiments show that only for the relation proposition task their method provides significant gains over existing methods, that too in the fully supervised mode.    For scene categorization their method is good only with supervision on attention relation. For object detection their gains are insignificant and for text classification they show gains only with the labeled data is small.

I have the following concerns about this work:
1.  Computing pairwise attention is computationally expensive, and the gains they obtain seem too small to justify.  The only significant gains are for the relation proposal task where such pairwise attention is expected to be the norm.

2.  Their experiments do not perform a fair comparison over the number of parameters and running time.   The FAN module inserts lot more parameters and quadratically blows up the attention vector length.  If we normalize on the number of  parameters and running time, it is unclear if the gains of FAN over  baseline will continue to hold.  For example, in the document classification task, they concatenate the FAN descriptor with usual  word to sentence attention.  What if a multi-headed attention is  used on the word to sentence layer? It is unclear if FAN will score over multi-headed attention.

3. Their coverage of related work and empirical comparison with existing work is sketchy.
Authors have not done justice to the multiple prior work that seek to
supervise attention or model the relationship between attention of
multiple entities.  Several papers on supervising attention but in the section 
"Attention Networks – Limitations" the authors do not mention these.  I list some of these:

Syntax-Directed Attention for Neural Machine Translation
Kehai Chen, Rui Wang, Masao Utiyama, Eiichiro Sumita, Tiejun Zhao
AAAI 2018.

Siddhesh Khandelwal, Leonid Sigal: AttentionRNN: A Structured Spatial
Attention Mechanism. CoRR abs/1905.09400 (2019)

Attentive Relational Networks for Mapping Images to Scene Graphs
Mengshi Qi, Weijian Li, Zhengyuan Yang, Yunhong Wang, Jiebo Luo; The IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 2019, pp. 3957-3966

Supervised Attentions for Neural Machine Translation
Haitao Mi Zhiguo Wang Abe Ittycheriah
https://www.aclweb.org/anthology/D16-1249.pdf


Question for authors:
---------------------------------
Please clarify the exact way in which the FAN module that provides word-pair
attention is converted into a sentence descriptor. From Figure~3 it appears that you do row-wise
max-pooling but please  specify clearly in section 4.5,  preferably with a formula.

The form of Equation 3 needs more justification. Why this specific form?

Presentation:
------------------
The first section is hard to read and requires significant improvement in writing.  I give some suggestions:

Typo in sentence:
"for the task of learning relationship attention weights between entities"

"relation weights" is an awkward construct.

A citation is required on "Relation Networks" in their first mention in this sentence:
" Typical qualitative examples comparing Relation Networks with our
Focused Attention Network are shown in Figure 1, with a quantitative
comparison reported in Section 5."

The sentences in the paper are often hard to parse.  Here is are some
examples:

"The scaled dot product attention module of Vaswani et al. (2017), for
example, uses learned pairwise attention weights between region
proposal network (RPN) generated bounding boxes in images of natural
scenes (Hu et al., 2018) to boost object detection."

"In fact, for a given reference object (region), relation networks (Hu
et al., 2018) tend to predict high attention weights with scaled or
shifted bounding boxes surrounding the same object instance. This is
likely because including surrounding context, or simply restoring
missing parts of the reference object, boosts object detection"

The illustration of attention in Figure 2 is not at all clear.

content.title: Response to Review #3
content.comment:
1. Regarding computational cost, the core contribution of our paper is a way to supervise the attention networks to better capture relationships between entities. The baseline that we are comparing against, is regular attention networks, where the need for computing attention weights is also present. It is widely demonstrated in the literature that using an attention mechanism and computing the attention weights for feature aggregation is beneficial. For instance, relation networks [2] used an attention module on top of F-RCNN [1] to boost detection performance and Vaswani et al 2017 [3] originally proposed this attention mechanism and demonstrated a non-trivial improvement over the baseline on a machine translation task. The above approaches all have the need to compute pair-wise attention weights. Thus we do not see the computation of these weights in our work as being a weakness.

2. The reviewer asks for an analysis of computational cost between regular attention networks and our focused attention networks. During the forward pass, the cost is exactly the same for a regular attention network and our focused attention network, since we introduce a new loss term that directly supervises the attention weights during back-propagation. This means that in practical applications, FAN does NOT incur any additional run time or space cost. During back propagation, we would need to compute gradients of the relation loss w.r.t parameters in each layer. This would in theory increase the training time, but in practice both a regular attention network and FAN take around 4 hours to finish 8 epochs of training. If this remains a significant concern for the reviewer and it might change his or her opinion of our paper, we would be happy to conduct a careful ablation study on model run times, comparing the regular attention network and FAN.

3. Regarding the concern about a fair comparison, again, we emphasize the fact that the attention module applied in our focused attention network IS exactly the same as that in regular attention networks that we aim to compare against (resembling [2][3]). The difference is that FAN is supervised by one additional loss term, the centre mass loss proposed in section 3. In our experiments, we made sure that the unsupervised cases (regular attention networks) have exactly the same structure and parameter sets as the supervised case (FAN as proposed in this paper). 

4. We will make sure to cite the very recent related papers mentioned by the reviewer, and to provide a careful discussion of them. We thank the reviewer for bringing these to our attention.

5. We appreciate that the construction of the sentence level descriptor is not described as well as it could be in Section 4.5, mainly due to space limitations. We will definitely address this in the next revision, before the discussion period ends. For now, please consider the following elaboration. Every FAN module applied in Figure 3 shares the same structure of Figure 3 top, as is explained in the text in Section 4.2 (FAN backbone). Thus, the sentence level embedding is computed as follows. The FAN module will compute the word-to-word attention matrix W and output its row-softmax version for attention aggregation, which is denoted as W_{agg}. Assume that we have N words in a sentence, and the word embedding dimension is 100. Now, W_{agg} has dimension of N by N and F_{in} is the input word embedding matrix which has dimension of N by 100. The attention aggregated output F_{out} = W_{agg} F_{in}, with a dimension of N by 100. We then use a max pooling to select the most dominant response in the attention aggregated embedding space, to serve as a supportive representation of the sentence level, on top of the original sentence level embedding from Hierarchical Attention Networks [4].

6. Regarding the concern for Equation 3’s design choice, we point out that we included a thorough model ablation study on loss function design in our original submission’s main text. Please see Table 3 in Section 5.3 and its related text for details. This ablation study is referred to in Section 3.3, when we discuss the loss functions for the first time in the paper. 

7. Regarding the two sentences which the reviewer found hard to parse, we would be happy to break these into simpler sentences which better convey the points we wished to make. However, despite the imperfect presentation, we do not think that this prose is critical to the main contributions of our paper.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
Summary:
The following work proposes some effective and simple pseudo-labels for graph attention on both vision and language tasks. The supervision provided by these heuristic-based allows the final model to outperform the unsupervised attention baseline. Results are demonstrated on the relationship proposal task, object detection (attention is applied to context encoding for each object), and scene categorization, and document categorization. The largest gains appear to be on the relationship proposal task, with small improvements over SOTA on all other tasks.


Strengths:
- The paper was fairly easy to follow
- The proposed automatic attention labeling schemes appear to be simple and effective
- Results demonstrated improvements on a variety of tasks.


Weaknesses and questions:
-For visual recognition datasets, the attention targets are defined such that we want to maximize the weights between two overlapping objects of differing classes. This seems very dataset/task specific, and clearly would not apply to other datasets such as human-human interaction datasets.
-I'm not sure that the center-mass CE loss is strictly a cross entropy loss? Maybe it would be if one takes the log of \tilde{\mathcal{W}} in (2) .
-Should center-mass be center-of-mass instead?
-The proposed center of mass seems to be a straightforward weighted reduced sum. I'm not sure where the "notion of center-mass" comes into play, nor how this is a novel contribution
-The pairing scheme for language tasks as shown in Figure 2 seems fairly arbitrary. Has this been properly ablated? How much does each particular pairing matter? How much better is it than some pairing scheme that includes the negative set of edges (verb-adjectiv, noun-adverb)?
-Any form of failure mode analysis is missing from this work. Figure 1 shows qualitative examples of when the proposed focused attention network performs qualitatively better than the Relation Network from Hu et al, but it's hard to believe that this is always the case.


Overall, I don't see the proposed loss, nor the conclusion that supervised attention (even with heuristic-based labels) can outperform unsupervised attention to be sufficient contributions. I do think that the discovery of a simple and effective pseudo-labeling scheme (creating edges for overlapping objects of differing classes) to yield some insight. That said, this is certainly much task specific, and such a similarly simple attention labeling strategy may not exist for other vision tasks.

content.title: Response to Review #1
content.comment:
1. We agree that when we construct the target exactly as described in section 3.2, it will not favour tasks when interactions between objects belonging to the same category are of interest. But this is not a limitation of the core method itself. Depending on the task at hand we could easily construct a supervision target by only pairing object pairs within the same category, and in doing so it is entirely possible that we could capture human-to-human interactions just as well. We point out that we included additional experiments on the effect of using different supervision targets in our experiments (Table 7 for a vision task and Table 8 for a language task). The user is free to construct the target in whatever manner he/she desires in our module. To demonstrate our good faith, we would be willing to conduct additional experiments to alleviate the reviewers’ concerns. We invite the reviewer to suggest a dataset of interest and we will try our best to provide results on supervising an attention target in a manner that is different than that in section 3.2.

2. Regarding our use of the term "`cross-entropy" loss in the name, we understand the concern of the reviewer. Indeed, we have log(M) and we optimize this term exclusively. We do not optimize log(1 - M). Perhaps renaming the loss to simply centre mass loss would be appropriate.

3. Regarding the name ``centre mass’’,  we define M = \tilde{\mathcal{W}} \odot T and name M as “the centre mass” because 1) it is the mass (or summation of entries) within W that is selected by the supervision target and 2) we would like this mass to be the major component of W, or namely its centre, because we optimize the centre mass loss to increase M. Thus, the reduced sum of M should ideally capture a large proportion of the reduced sum of W. As the reviewer suggests, perhaps ``centre-of-mass’’ would be a better choice of term. 

4. Regarding the novelty, there are multiple ways to supervise the attention weights, for example, we can directly supervise each entry in the matrix W to penalize it or increase it, depending on the supervision target. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose supervising the attention weights on a matrix scale, that is considering all possible relationship pairs that may occur in an image (or sentence). In Table 1 we report on different manners of supervision, including supervising a row instead of a matrix, or supervising a matrix without the focal term. We find that a matrix scale supervision on the centre mass is better than supervision on a row, and using the focal loss term prevents a domination by a few big attention values in the matrix, which could lead to problematic local minima. Each individual design choice is supported with a careful ablation study, in either Table 1 or Table 3 (where we further consider different loss functions for supervising the centre mass). 

5. We included ablation study on different pairing schemes for the language task in appendix A, due space limitations. Please see Table 8 (on page 11 bottom) where we considered a document classification task with different word-to-word supervision targets constructed. We considered four different supervision targets, each with a careful definition in the text supporting Table 8. If required by the reviewer, we could run additional ablation study experiments following this line of trials.

6. We indeed have failure modes when we inspect the relation weight learning results, between baseline attention networks and the ones with focus. We could certainly include such visualizations in our appendix. Please let us know if this is desirable and we will work on this ASAP.

Within the space limitations of a conference paper, we are able to demonstrate improvements over 4 diverse downstream tasks. Thus it is entirely possible that researchers from other fields might find focusing the attention being beneficial in their line of work. We are by no means claiming to beat the standard attention networks in terms of performance, but rather, we are proposing a low-cost attention supervision technique that is very simple to apply and which can benefit multiple tasks.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
Attention models has been extensively used to achieve state-of-the-art performance in computer vision and natural language processing. This paper identifies a problem that the attention weights in the standard models tend to concentrate on single or very few locations which fails to reflect relations between entities. The main contribution of the paper is to introduce a relation module in the neural network's architecture and a relation loss to enhance learning relations between different entities. Experiments are conducted on several benchmark tasks including object detection, scene categorization and document categorization to show the effectiveness of the method. 

One major concern I have is about the novelty of the method. In particular, the center-mass cross entropy loss, which is one of the central component in the paper, is indeed the same as the focal loss in [1]. The only difference is to apply it on a matrix to measure relations. This makes the contribution limited. Moreover, I also have some concerns about the experiments, which will be detailed in the following. Overall, I find the paper has interesting observations and results, but the paper is not easy to follow and the contribution is limited. I am willing to increase my score if my concerns are clarified. 

a. About the training of the relation matrix  
One of the key component of the algorithm is to train a relation matrix between entities. I have a few concerns about this step. 

First, are the entities given by a pre-trained model or is it learned during the training? If these entities are learned, then how do we train the relation matrix? For example let's say they are region of interests (ROI), the region proposal will be very poor at the beginning and the correct regions may not be included so how to handle the relation matrix between these poor regions? Moreover, how do we use the ground truth regions since maybe some of them are not correctly identified even in the well-trained model. 

Second, do we need extra annotations to learn the relation matrix? In particular, the information of relations is needed in order to train the relation matrix, this does not seem to be free from since we need to distinguish whether they are the same instances. This would make the comparison to other models unfair since more information are available here. 

b. About the comparison to the benchmarks
I am not an expert of the tasks considered in the paper so I may not notice the sensitivity of the improvement.  

In the object detection task, I would expect a better state-of-the-art performance since F-RCNN seems to be a weak baseline. The second column of the object detection table is using FAN + L_{det}, but it cites the Relation Network [2], is this a better baseline comparing to the Relation Network? What are the differences?

[1] Focal loss for dense object detection, Lin et al, 2017
[2] Relation networks for object detection, Hu et al 2018

content.title: Response to Review #2
content.comment:
1. Our article does indeed involve an application of focal loss on a measurement we defined as centre mass, on a matrix form. However, we emphasize that the novelty is NOT in applying the focal loss, but rather, in a proposal for supervising the defined centre mass, in a matrix manner, to better capture relationships between entities in the data. This involves the construction of a supervision target, as defined in section 3.2 and its element-wise multiplication with the attention matrix W, which yields the centre mass that we aim to increase during optimization. In addition, we carefully conducted model ablation studies using different forms of loss functions to optimize the learning of the centre mass in Table 3 of section 5.3. In summary, we propose a strategy to increase the centre mass during neural network learning, not simply the application of a previously proposed loss function on a matrix, as stated by the reviewer. In fact, even with the use of possibly superior loss functions, our centre mass supervision will still likely improve the attention weight learning/specific task performance. 

2. Regarding the entities in the data, let us assume the object detection case, where these entities come from a RPN (region proposal network). We train our detection models end-to-end from scratch, that is, we do not use a pre-trained detection/RPN network to get the entities. Thus, at the beginning, the RPN does not generate good proposals and few of these have overlap with ground truth bounding boxes. This will result in all the entries in the supervision target in section 3.2 being zero, thus making the centre mass zero. During back propagation, therefore, the relation loss will not influence the weight learning of the network. However, once the RPN begins to converge (after the second epoch or so, the total number of epochs being 8 in our experiments), the relation loss starts to kick in because we have valid supervision targets. Indeed, proper balancing between the relation loss and the main task loss is required.  In our experiments, we used the loss weighting scheme discussed in Section C of the appendix.

3. When the RPN fails to capture a ground truth bounding box, then our network will also fail to capture its possible relationships as well as its detection. This is a universal weakness, shared with the regular attention networks as well as with F-RCNN.

4. We emphasize that we absolutely DO NOT need any annotations of relation labels to learn plausible relationships/attention weights. This is the core strength of our approach, as carefully demonstrated by our relation proposal task experiments. We achieve the same performance as the past state-of-the-art WITHOUT using the relation annotations on Visual Genome dataset (see Table 2). In order to construct a supervision target matrix we simply use the object’s class label. We allow two instances to have a possible relationship when they belong to different object classes. Figure 4 in appendix A provides a visual understanding of how we build this supervision target. 

5. We have not claimed that boosting detection is a major contribution of FAN. Rather, it is the versatility of the FAN module in application to diverse tasks including relation proposals, detection, scene classification and document classification. Taken together, our experiments demonstrate that the core idea of supervising the centre mass (attention) is beneficial for all these tasks. To address the concerns of the reviewer we clarify that FAN + L_{det} is basically the setup of Relation Networks [2], but in our implementation. Relation networks [2] is a stronger baseline than F-RCNN, and is also the unsupervised case of FAN. The comparison of FAN + L_{det} with FAN + L_{det} + L_{rel} is just to show the additional benefit of supervising the relation learning with the proposed centre mass loss.

content.title: Re: Response to Review #2
content.comment: Thanks for the clarification. I am still very confused about how the supervision of the weight matrix is done. It is claimed there is no need of annotations of relation labels, then what are the supervised labels for the weight matrix? Could you provide a more precise explanation in the object detection case about how the weight matrix are supervised? More concretely, what are the labels used in the training?

replying_to: Replying to Re: Response to Review #2

content.title: More on Supervision Label Construction
content.comment:
Thanks for your continued interest! To understand exactly how we used no relation labels, but still constructed a supervision target in matrix form, please take a look at Figure 4 in the appendix. Once we have generated N proposals from RPN, we match these proposals with the ground truth blue and orange boxes. Here we ONLY use an object's class label.

Let's say proposal "a" matches the human in a blue box and proposal "b" matches with the sheep in an orange box, and both have a IOU > 0.5 with the ground-truth. We then consider there to be a "potential relationship" between proposal "a" and "b", and we assign T[a,b] = 1. That is, as long as two proposals are matched to objects from different categories, we would assign "1" to the T matrix for this entry. We then iterate over all possible (a,b) pairs from the N * N possible pairings between object proposals, to finish building the T matrix.

Later on, we multiply T with W element-wise, to only select those entries that may have a potential relationship.  This selected proportion of W is reduce-summed to acquire mass M and sent into the center mass loss to increase the selected attention weights. In this fashion, during the training, more commonly observed object pairs in ground truth data will occur more frequently in T matrices, and thus get emphasized. Thus, throughout the process, no explicit relationship labels are used.

We hope this makes things clearer.
